heard: A missing hyphen did not actually destroy NASA's first interplanetary rocket. On July 22, 1962, Mariner 1 launched toward Venus aboard an Atlas-Agena rocket. At 293 seconds, wild steering corrections forced a safety officer to detonate the spacecraft. Author Arthur C. Clarke in press accounts famously blamed a missing hyphen in guidance code. In reality, programmers omitted a single mathematical overbar above the letter R in guidance equations. Without that smoothing bar, the computer treated minor radar noise as violent velocity fluctuations. That exact code had flown safely on lunar missions, but an in-flight hardware failure triggered the flaw. Five weeks later Mariner 2 reached Venus, proving Space History's most famous typo was not a hyphen.
